name: Carla Nakamura

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Carla. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to anything. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at the distribution centre for a home-improvement chain, the bulky side. I ride a low-level order picker, which is like a pallet truck you stand on, and I pick paint tins, bags of tile adhesive, flat-pack wardrobes and the odd bathtub onto pallets for the stores. Shifts are two till ten, Monday to Friday.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's physical and you can see what you've done, a full pallet wrapped and labelled. What wears me out is lifting twenty-kilo bags all evening, and the fact they cut overtime since the housing market slowed down. I share a flat with my friend Jo, who's a dental nurse, and I'm single, so it's my wage paying my half.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, I never thought a chatbot was going to lift a bathtub. At work we'd shrug. I might share a funny meme about it in the group chat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, AI isn't my problem, the overtime is. Since they cut the overtime, I've lost about two hundred a month. That was my savings money. I've got about three months saved and it's not growing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my shifts and look for weekend work, maybe at the garden centre down the road. I'd cut the gym membership, because I lift enough at work anyway. And I'd ask my manager about the day-shift team leader opening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. Nothing's wrong, but nothing's getting better either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill goes first if money gets tighter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car insurance renewal comes in April, and it's gone up every year. I'd probably switch to the bus, but the last bus home is before my shift ends. So I'd be stuck paying it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the team leader opening. Would you go for it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, yeah. I'm not sure I want to be the one chasing people for rates. But it's more money and it's days, so I'd have a life.

say: I'd say I never thought a **chatbot** would lift a bathtub.
I'd share a **funny meme** in the work group chat and shrug.
think: AI isn't my problem, the **overtime cut** is.
I've lost about **two hundred** a month and my savings aren't growing.
do: Look for **weekend work** at the garden centre down the road.
Ask about the day-shift **team leader** opening.

fieldNote: Her pressure comes from **lost overtime**, not technology.
As a **single earner** she feels each cost directly.
Her late shift traps her into keeping the **car**.
She is **unsure** about becoming a team leader who chases rates.

steps.text: Find weekend work at the garden centre down the road
Apply for the day-shift team leader opening

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's sensible to use it where it helps, but don't pretend it's going to do everything. I'd probably say that online, calmly, if anyone asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the office would change, the people doing store orders and the planners. My side is bulky and awkward, so robots would take a long time to manage it. They trialled an automatic storage system for small items last year, but nobody's touched the bathtubs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going and save a bit more, back to a hundred a month if I get weekend work. I'd start using the AI app on my phone for budgeting, because Jo uses one and swears by it. And I'd keep the team leader idea on the table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, the same as now really. It's change happening a floor above me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said nobody's touched the bathtubs. How sure are you of that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not very, honestly. I've seen videos of robots that lift big things. The forklifts in our warehouse are fifteen years old, so I don't see the company spending millions on robots soon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mate Lena in the office does store replenishment, working out what each shop needs. That's exactly the planning AI would do. Lena (her friend) has already said she's thinking of coming down to the floor.

say: I'd say use AI **where it helps** but don't pretend it does everything.
I'd say it **calmly** online if anyone asked.
think: The **office** changes first: store orders and planners.
**Bulky goods** like bathtubs will take robots a long time.
do: Save a bit more, back to **a hundred** a month with weekend work.
Use an **AI budgeting app** like Jo does.

fieldNote: She judges **bulky goods** as hard to automate, which keeps her steadier.
She sees office **planning roles** as the first to go.

steps.text: Save a hundred a month again from weekend shifts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too fast and the government has to step in, with retraining and some kind of support. I'm not usually political, but I would be then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be scared, because I'm single and it's just my wage. The office goes in 2028, and the robots that lift bathtubs come around 2031. I'd be thirty with no qualifications past school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a dental nursing course straight away, because Jo says they're always short and it's working with people. I'd keep my warehouse shifts while I train, evenings at the warehouse and days at college. I'd cut back to the bone and sell the car if I can get a day job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. My stomach turns, because I don't have anyone else's wage to fall back on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you really do college and warehouse shifts at once?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For a year, maybe. Jo did her course while working in a café. It'd be hard, but I'd rather be tired than stuck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would dental nursing be safe, with robots coming in 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know. I think people want a person holding their hand in the dentist's chair, at least for a while. It's a guess, but it's a better guess than the warehouse.

say: I'd say it's **too fast** and the government must step in.
I'd want **retraining** and support, and I'd become political.
think: I'm **single**, so it's just my wage at risk.
The **bathtub robots** come around 2031, when I'm thirty with no qualifications.
do: Start a **dental nursing course** straight away.
Keep **evening shifts** at the warehouse while studying.
Sell the **car** if I get a day job.
feel: **Alarmed**, with **no other wage** to fall back on.
S2.quote: I'd rather be tired than stuck.
fieldNote: Being a **single earner** sharpens her fear.
She uses the **three-year gap** to train while still earning.
**Jo's career** gives her a tested path into dental nursing.
She admits dental nursing is only **a better guess**.

steps.text: Enrol on a dental nursing course this year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to plan properly, so let's not panic. But I'd want the company to tell us its plans early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'd have until about 2034 in the warehouse. That's long enough to save up and do the dental nursing course without killing myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend the first year getting savings to five months. Then I'd start the dental nursing course part time in 2028, keeping my shifts. I'd ask HR if the company has any training money for people leaving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a way I can handle. It's a plan with dates on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you give up to save those five months?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Holidays, mostly, and eating out with Jo on Fridays. I'd keep my Sunday swim, though, because that's what keeps me sane.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said let's not panic in public. Are you calm in private?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, not really. But panicking at work doesn't help anyone. I'd rather quietly get on with it.

fieldNote: She shows a clear **gap** between public calm and private worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a fair amount of time, and people should use it. I wouldn't make a big thing of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's fine for me. I could save, train and be a qualified dental nurse by about 2031, well before the robots come for bulky goods in 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go for the team leader job first, to earn more for a couple of years. Then I'd do the dental nursing course around 2029. I'd keep using the budgeting app and try out other AI tools once I see them working for Jo.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but okay. Ten years is the one picture where I feel I can steer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why team leader first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: More money now means more savings later. And it'd look good on a CV, showing I can manage people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you miss about the warehouse?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The quiet satisfaction of a wrapped pallet. And the crew on lates, we have a pizza night on the last Friday of the month. I'd miss that.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because I'm on my own and there's no time to train. What would help is free part-time courses and a bit of money while you study, so single people aren't choosing between rent and college.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about being single in all this. People talk about families, which is fair, but when it's just you, there's no second wage. That's what keeps me careful.

headlineQuote: When it's just you, there's no second wage.
portrait: Carla is a **27-year-old picker** on the bulky side of a home-improvement distribution centre.
She is single, shares a flat with **Jo**, a dental nurse, and has about three months saved.
Lost **overtime** already squeezes her before AI enters the picture.
She believes **bulky goods** are slow to automate, which keeps her steadier in milder pictures.
Her plan is **dental nursing**, timed to how much warning she gets.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she's a single earner with no time to train.
whatWouldHelp: **Free part-time courses** with some income while studying.
